en.title: VisionQuest Just Introduced Marvel's Very First Hero, And It's Complicated
en.summary: The MCU has long considered Iron Man its origin point, but a recent episode of VisionQuest has officially brought the original Marvel Comics hero into the fold. This historic moment, however, comes with a tangled web of comic book history.
en.body:
For years, the narrative has been clear: **Tony Stark** was the spark that ignited the modern superhero era in the MCU. But as **VisionQuest** season 1 episode 7, titled "Immolation," has just revealed, the *actual* first hero in the Marvel universe predates Iron Man by decades. The Human Torch, a flaming android first created by **Carl Burgos**, has officially made his MCU debut, finally aligning the cinematic timeline with the very first issue of Marvel Comics from 1939.

This isn't just a simple cameo; the Human Torch, an enduring character from the Golden Age of comics and a founding member of the **All-Winners Squad**, brings a significant legacy with him. He was a flagship character for Timely Comics, the precursor to Marvel, starring in his own series and appearing alongside other early icons like Captain America and Namor. His introduction into **VisionQuest**, a series delving into **Vision's** own existential crisis and featuring **James Spader's** return as **Ultron**, suggests a narrative that aims to explore the very foundations of heroism and artificial life within the MCU.

## The Torch's Fiery Legacy

The arrival of the Human Torch is more than just a nod to comic history; it's a complex narrative choice. The character's journey through Timely Comics, from fighting gangsters to battling Nazis alongside his sidekick Toro, established him as a foundational figure. His integration into **VisionQuest** raises immediate questions about how this Golden Age hero will interact with the established MCU continuity, especially considering the series' focus on **Vision's** evolving identity and his complex relationship with **Ultron**. The implications for Phase Six of the MCU are significant, potentially opening doors to further explorations of Marvel's earliest heroes and their impact on the universe we've come to know.

## Fan Reaction and Future Implications

The fan community is already abuzz with speculation following the "Immolation" episode. For long-time comic readers, seeing the original Human Torch finally appear in the MCU is a moment many have anticipated for years. The decision to introduce him in **VisionQuest**, a series that is already grappling with profound themes of existence and artificial intelligence, suggests a deliberate effort to connect the MCU's past with its present and future. The intricate history of the Human Torch, from his solo adventures to his role in early superhero teams, provides fertile ground for future storytelling. Fans are eager to see how this foundational character will influence the ongoing narrative and what other Golden Age figures might follow.

## What's Next

**VisionQuest** continues its eight-episode run on Disney+, with new episodes dropping weekly until its conclusion on November 10. The presence of the Human Torch has undoubtedly set the stage for a deeper dive into Marvel's rich history, leaving fans to wonder what other surprises await in the remaining episodes.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for VisionQuest season 1 episode 7 . In the MCU , the first superhero is effectively Iron Man . Sure, Nick Fury tells him he isn’t the first at the end of the 2008 movie, and we know that Captain Marvel , the Eternals , and others predate him. But for all intents and purposes, it starts with Tony Stark. In Marvel Comics, however, it starts with the Human Torch, a flaming android who appears on the cover of 1939’s Marvel Comics #1. Now the MCU has finally caught up, with the Human Torch officially debuting in the latest episode of VisionQuest , “Immolation.” But as anyone familiar with the Fantastic Four has already realized, the history of the Human Torch is complicated, and his insertion into the VisionQuest storyline only makes things more so. Created by Carl Burgos, the Human Torch was a mainstay of Golden Age comics published by Timely, the company that would eventually become Marvel. One of the company’s first breakout stars, the Human Torch not only moved quickly into his own (admittedly, short-lived) solo series in 1940, but he regularly appeared in other anthologies and team-up books, including Marvel Mystery Comics , All Winners , Young Allies , and Young Men . Like most Golden Age heroes, he initially fought gangsters and racketeers before shifting to Nazis and other Axis soldiers, battling them at home and abroad. It was in that latter capacity that the Human Torch helped form Marvel’s first superhero team, the All-Winners Squad, later renamed the Invaders. Alongside his teen sidekick Toro, a circus fire-eater who learned to also how to set his body ablaze, the Human Torch joined Captain America and Bucky, Namor, Miss America, and a yellow-clad hero called Whizzer (really) to battle against Axis powers wherever they found them. In fact, canonically, the Human Torch is the one who killed Hitler, burning the Nazi leader alive. That last point highlights the most interesting thing about the Human Torch and his position within the Marvel Universe. Ask any casual comic fan, and they’ll tell you that Marvel heroes have feet of clay, in contrast to the godlike icons of the DC Universe. Yet, most think of that distinction occurring when Timely, and its immediate predecessor Atlas, became Marvel Comics in the 1960s, with the birth of reluctant heroes such as the Hulk and Spider-Man . Captain America, with his blond hair and lantern jaw, seemed more like a classic DC -style hero in the Golden Age. But the Human Torch’s first appearance in Marvel Comics #1 undermines that assumption, proving that Marvel was interested in monsters even before it was Marvel. The first Human Torch story is very much a Frankenstein tale, complete with a mad scientist who fears his creation. The first half of the story follows scientist Phineas Horton as he seeks help in controlling his creation, a synthetic man whose skin goes ablaze whenever exposed to oxygen.
